 Meet BLUETTI APEX 200
 Apex 200 is a versatile, expandable portable power station designed for home backup, RV travel, and off-grid use. It delivers 2.56 kWh of capacity and 3,200W of continuous AC output on its own, with up to 3,600W available under supported conditions.* Compared with selected mainstream 3kWh portable power stations, Apex 200 is 20% lighter and 50% smaller by volume, making it easier to move between your home, RV, and campsite.* Add compatible expansion batteries when you need longer backup. 
 Big Enough For Home Backup And RV Power
 With 2,560Wh of capacity, 10 output ports, and 3,200–3,600W of continuous AC output, Apex 200 can power multiple compatible home essentials and RV devices at once.* 
 Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.
 Start with 2.56 kWh for home essentials like your refrigerator, lights, and Wi-Fi. If an outage lasts longer, add compatible B300K or B500K batteries for more runtime. When you need to run more household equipment at once, connect multiple Apex 200 systems using the required Hub A1 and compatible accessories—scaling up to 99.84 kWh of capacity and 6,000W of combined output.* Build on the system you already have instead of replacing it as your power needs grow. 
 Up To 3,000 W Dual-Input Solar Charging
 Bring in more solar energy and recharge faster off grid. Apex 200 supports up to 2,000W through the high-voltage MC4 input and up to 1,000W through the low-voltage XT60 input, reaching 80% in about 50 minutes and a full charge in about 1.7 hours under specified conditions. The 60–280V high-voltage MPPT range supports compatible panels connected in series, helping simplify solar wiring.* 
 RV Power, Built Right In.
 Connect a compatible RV through the TT-30R outlet, and power 12V gear such as a refrigerator, water pump, lights, and fans through the 12V/30A Anderson output. 
 Monitor, Control, And Schedule Your Power.
 The BLUETTI app does more than show battery level and charging status. Control supported AC outlets individually, schedule when devices run, stop nonessential loads at a selected battery level, use TOU mode to charge during lower-rate hours, and receive severe weather alerts with the option to enable automatic charging. Compatible with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant. 
 Smart AC Outlet Control 
 Turn supported AC outlets on or off remotely, set schedules, or stop nonessential loads at a selected battery level. 
 Charge When Electricity Costs Less 
 Set TOU charging in the BLUETTI app to help reduce charging costs during lower-rate hours. 
 Get Severe Weather Alerts 
 Receive alerts and choose whether to enable automatic charging before a potential outage. 
 Recharge At Home, On The Road, Or Off Grid.
 Long-Lasting Power, Protected From The Inside.
 Long-life LiFePO₄ battery cells are designed for years of dependable use, while an intelligent battery management system monitors operating conditions, helps manage heat, and protects key components during charging and operation.*

 Product Notes 
 AC Output: Standalone continuous output is 3,200W. Up to 3,600W continuous output requires compatible expansion batteries or supported AC/solar input conditions. 
 Energy Density: Compared with selected 3 kWh-class power stations, 20% refers to gravimetric energy density (Wh/kg) and 50% to volumetric energy density (Wh/L), not direct weight or volume reductions. 
 Solar Charging: Up to 3,000W combined input (2,000W high-voltage + 1,000W low-voltage) requires compatible solar configurations. Actual charging performance varies with sunlight, panel setup, and operating conditions. 
 Battery Expansion: Each Apex 200 supports up to six compatible expansion batteries. Maximum capacity of 99.84kWh and combined output of 6,000W require three Apex 200 units, eighteen B500K batteries, Hub A1, and compatible accessories, sold separately. 
 Fast Charging: Maximum AC charging power requires a compatible high-power AC connection and specified charging cable. Actual input depends on outlet, circuit, and configuration. Charging times are based on BLUETTI internal testing and may vary. Some charging methods require additional accessories. 
 UPS Backup: UPS mode must be enabled in the BLUETTI app. Automatic switching applies to properly connected devices. Transfer performance varies by operating conditions and may not meet every device's requirements. 
 Smart AC Control: Outlet control, scheduling, and battery-level automation require compatible settings in the BLUETTI app. Feature availability may vary by firmware and connectivity. 
 Battery Life & Safety: Cycle-life figures are based on BLUETTI laboratory testing to 70% of original battery capacity. Actual results vary. UL 94 5VA applies only to specified materials or components, not the complete system.

BLUETTI Apex 200 Review: 2.56kWh Home and RV Power Station 
 Skip to content 
 Dan Miller 
 Home Backup Editor 
 Last updated November 5, 2026
 Covers home backup: outage prep, running essentials, and picking the right unit for your household.
 Most people shopping for a big power station want it to do two jobs: keep the fridge and Wi-Fi running when the grid goes down, and power a camper on weekends. Until now, BLUETTI’s answer for both was the Apex 300, a capable unit that weighs almost 84 lb. The BLUETTI Apex 200 , announced on October 21, 2026, is the lighter take on that idea.
 In this guide 16 sections · 16 min read 
 1 
 Quick Verdict 
 2 
 Apex 200 vs Apex 300: What Changed 
 3

 It packs 2,560Wh of LFP battery and 3,200W of 120V output into a 59.3 lb box, with a TT-30R RV outlet and a 12V/30A Anderson port built in. It takes up to 3,000W of solar and expands to 33.28kWh with add-on batteries. It joins a growing BLUETTI power station lineup that now runs from pocket-size units to modular home systems.
 One thing to know up front: the Apex 200 is 120V only. It has no 240V output, so it cannot run a well pump, an electric dryer or central air. That single spec decides most Apex 200 vs Apex 300 choices, and we cover it in detail below.
 A note on method: this is a spec-based analysis, not a hands-on test. Every figure comes from BLUETTI’s product page and user manual, attributed as such, or from our own math, which we show. We have no owner data yet.
 2,560Wh LFP capacity expandable to 33.28kWh 
 3,200W 120V output up to 3,600W, see below 
 3,000W solar input high- and low-voltage inputs 
 59.3 lb weight two-hand carry 
 New for 2026 BLUETTI Apex 200
 2,560Wh · 3,200W output · Price tracked daily since Sep 26
 $1,099 $1,399 -21% 
 2,560Wh LFP, 3,200W at 120V, TT-30R and Anderson ports built in, with a 5-year warranty.
 See the deal on BLUETTI Read our review 
 Quick Verdict 
 In three lines 
 Get the Apex 200 if you split your time between home outages and a 30A RV, and you want plenty of solar input on a station you can still move.
 Get the Apex 300 if anything in your house runs on 240V, or if you plan to wire a backup system into your panel.
 Compare the prices: $1,099 for the Apex 200 against $1,499 for the Apex 300, with the same 5-year warranty.
 BLUETTI Apex 200: BPH Rating
 8.5 /10 
 “The Apex 300 idea, made lighter and ready for the RV”
 Capacity & expansion 9.0 
 Solar input 9.0 
 RV readiness 9.0 
 Power output 8.0 
 Portability 7.5 
 Launch value 8.5 
 Spec-based rating, reviewed on November 4, 2026 with the launch price. Updated when owner data are available.
 Pick the Apex 200 if you…
 want one station for home outages and a 30A RV 
 want up to 3,000W of solar input on a movable unit
 want USB-C, 12V and Anderson ports without buying a hub
 plan to start at 2.56kWh and add batteries later 
 Look elsewhere if you…
 need 240V for a well pump, dryer or central air
 have a 50A RV and want to power all of it
 want full-speed AC charging without buying an extra cable
 want wheels or a one-hand carry 
 Apex 200 vs Apex 300: What Changed 
 The Apex 200 is not a cut-down Apex 300 across the board. BLUETTI kept the same fast charging and the same expansion batteries, then traded the 240V output for a lighter body, more solar input and built-in RV ports. BLUETTI’s own FAQ sums it up: the Apex 200 is the more movable 120V system , the Apex 300 is for a more advanced home backup setup with 120V/240V . Here is how the specs line up, with Apex 300 figures from our BLUETTI Apex 300 review .
 Spec Apex 200 Apex 300 
 Capacity 2,560Wh LFP 2,764.8Wh LFP 
 AC output 3,200W (up to 3,600W with an add-on battery) 3,840W 
 Power Lifting (resistive loads) 5,400W 7,680W 
 Voltage 120V only 120V and 240V 
 AC outlets 3× NEMA 5-20R, 1× TT-30R 4× 20A, 1× TT-30R, 1× NEMA 14-50R 
 USB, 12V, Anderson Built in Requires the Hub D1 
 Solar input 3,000W (2,000W at 60-280V + 1,000W low-voltage) 2,400W (2× 1,200W at 12-60V) 
 AC charging 80% in 45 min (Turbo mode, optional 30A or 50A cable) 80% in 45 min 
 Cycle life 6,000+ to 70% capacity 6,000+ to 80% capacity 
 Expansion Up to 6 B300K or B500K Up to 6 expansion batteries 
 Weight 59.3 lb 83.78 lb 
 Dimensions 20.67 × 12.87 × 8.31 in 20.67 × 12.87 × 12.6 in 
 Warranty 5 years 5 years 
 Price $1,099 $1,499 
 Max solar input (W)
 BLUETTI Apex 200: 3,000
 BLUETTI Apex 300: 2,400
 Weight (lb)
 BLUETTI Apex 200: 59.3
 BLUETTI Apex 300: 83.78
 Lighter and smaller
 By our math, the Apex 200 is 29% lighter than the Apex 300 (59.3 lb against 83.78 lb) and takes up about 34% less space (36.2 liters against roughly 55). Two of the three dimensions are identical. The saving comes from the third: 8.31 in on the Apex 200, against 12.6 in on the Apex 300. BLUETTI describes it as a two-handed carry, with built-in handles.
 More solar, at higher voltage
 The Apex 200 accepts 3,000W of solar , 25% more than the Apex 300. It splits that across two inputs: 2,000W through a high-voltage MC4 input (60-280V) and 1,000W through a low-voltage XT60 input . The high-voltage input lets you wire panels in longer series strings, which means thinner cables and less loss over distance.
 Ports you don’t have to buy separately
 On the Apex 300, the USB, 12V and Anderson outputs live on the Hub D1, a $299 accessory on BLUETTI’s site (October 22, 2026). The Apex 200 has them built in: two USB-A at 15W, a 100W and a 140W USB-C, a 12V/10A car outlet and a 12V/30A Anderson port . For an RV, that Anderson port matters, and it is one less box to carry.
 What you give up: 240V and 640W
 The Apex 300 delivers 3,840W at 120V and 240V, with a NEMA 14-50R outlet. The Apex 200 delivers 3,200W on its own and stays at 120V. BLUETTI’s user manual gives 3,600W with an expansion battery connected; its product page adds that 3,600W is also possible with active AC or solar input. If you need 240V today or might later, the Apex 300 is the one to buy.
 The 240V option BLUETTI Apex 300
 2,765Wh · 3,840W output · Lowest tracked: $1,499 (Nov 4)

 What Stands Out 
 RV-ready out of the box
 The TT-30R outlet takes a standard 30A RV plug, so the Apex 200 can feed a travel trailer’s whole electrical panel. The 12V/30A Anderson port powers 12V gear directly. A 30A RV service is rated for 3,600W, while the Apex 200 delivers 3,200W on its own, so avoid running the air conditioner and the microwave at the same time. Our guide to 30A vs 50A RV power systems explains how to size the load.
 3,000W of dual solar input
 Few stations of this size take this much solar. With both inputs filled, BLUETTI says the Apex 200 reaches 80% in about 50 minutes and 100% in about 1.7 hours . That makes a meaningful difference off-grid, where a short sunny window has to refill the battery.
 Expandable to 33.28kWh, or about 100kWh with three units
 One Apex 200 accepts up to six B300K or B500K expansion batteries . With three units linked through BLUETTI’s Hub A1, the system reaches 6,000W and 99.84kWh , according to BLUETTI. You can start with a single unit and grow when your needs change. BLUETTI’s manual also shows an Apex 300 connected to the expansion port as a battery, for up to 7,440W and 5,324.8Wh.
 Smart outlets, TOU mode and weather alerts
 BLUETTI’s app controls four AC outlets individually : on and off remotely, on a schedule, or cut automatically when the battery falls to a level you choose. That last feature keeps the fridge running longer by dropping less important loads first. The app also offers a time-of-use mode to charge during cheaper hours, and severe weather alerts that ask before charging the battery ahead of a storm. BLUETTI lists Amazon Alexa, Google Home and Home Assistant compatibility on its product page.
 What Could Be Better 
 It’s 120V only
 No 240V means no well pump, electric dryer, electric range or central air. BLUETTI’s manual lists 120V outputs only, and describes linked units as a way to raise output to 6,000W. If your outage plan includes any of those, look at the Apex 300 or at our guide to whole-home backup battery systems .
 The cycle rating stops at 70%
 BLUETTI rates the Apex 200 for 6,000+ cycles to 70% capacity . The Apex 300 gets the same 6,000 cycles, but to 80%. Both are excellent in practice: one full cycle a day would take more than 16 years. The Apex 200’s rating is simply the more conservative of the two.
 Full-speed AC charging needs an extra cable
 The cable in the box uses the 15A input, which BLUETTI’s manual limits to 1,800W . The 80%-in-45-minutes figure needs Turbo mode and an optional TT-30P or NEMA 14-50P cable on the P050A port, rated at 3,200W. The manual also asks for an overcurrent protection device when you use Turbo charging.
 Noise and cold-weather charging
 BLUETTI lists 50 dB maximum . The unit discharges down to -4°F, but it only charges from 32°F to 104°F , which matters in a cold RV or garage. Our guide to power stations in freezing temperatures covers what to do.
 UPS is off by default
 The Apex 200 switches connected devices to battery within 15ms , according to BLUETTI, but UPS mode has to be turned on in the app first. BLUETTI’s manual says the feature is not meant for data servers or workstations that need a high-performance UPS, and that the product is not intended for applications such as medical equipment that demand very high power reliability.
 59.3 lb is a two-hand carry
 BLUETTI describes “secure, two-handed carrying” and advises asking for help when needed. The unit has no wheels, though its manual lists the Foldable Trolley 2 as an accessory. Moving it from the house to the RV is a job for two hands, or two people.
 Home Backup: What 2,560Wh Covers 
 For a typical outage, the Apex 200 is an essentials station . About 2,176Wh of usable energy keeps a refrigerator, the internet, lights and phones going through a night and most of the next day. Its 3,200W of output also starts the kitchen appliances smaller stations struggle with, like a microwave, a coffee maker or a toaster.
 For most outages, plan on plugging appliances in directly. BLUETTI says no electrician is needed for standalone use. A connection to a home panel is possible, but it requires compatible equipment and installation by a qualified electrician. BLUETTI also lists a launch bundle with two Apex 200 units, two B300K batteries, a Hub A1 and a Home Backup Kit.
 When an outage drags on, expansion batteries extend the runtime. According to BLUETTI, each B300K adds about 3 days of refrigerator runtime and each B500K about 5 days . Those figures assume an efficient fridge, so treat them as best-case numbers.
 RV and Off-Grid Use 
 Running a 30A RV from the TT-30R
 Plug the RV’s 30A cord into the Apex 200 and the whole coach runs on battery: lights, outlets, the water pump and the 120V side of the fridge. The limit is power, not plugs. A 13,500 BTU rooftop air conditioner draws roughly 1,400W while running and much more at start-up. BLUETTI’s manual lists surge handling of up to 4,800W for 10 seconds on a single unit, and warns that motors can draw 2 to 4 times their rated power when starting, so a soft starter on the AC is still a sensible precaution. The 5,400W Power Lifting mode is for resistive loads only, such as kettles and hair dryers, and it doesn’t help a compressor.
 Charging while you drive
 Paired with BLUETTI’s Charger 2 , which charges from the vehicle’s alternator, the Apex 200 refills to 100% in about 3 hours of driving , according to BLUETTI. The older Charger 1 takes about 5 hours.
 Campground and generator charging
 At a campground, BLUETTI offers optional cables from a TT-30P or NEMA 14-50P plug to the Apex 200’s P050A port, both rated at 3,200W. BLUETTI says Turbo mode refills the battery to 100% in about 1.6 hours . A compatible generator works too. For the wider picture, see our RV electrical system basics .
 Solar Charging: How Fast Can It Refill? 
 These are calculated estimates for an empty battery, using a 0.7 factor for real-world panel output.
 Hours of full sun ≈ 2,560Wh ÷ (solar watts × 0.7) Both inputs, 3,000W: about 1.2 h · High-voltage only, 2,000W: about 1.8 h · Low-voltage only, 1,000W: about 3.7 h 
 BLUETTI’s own examples line up with that math: about 2.2 hours to 100% with up to four 500W panels, 2.1 hours with up to six 350W panels, and 1.9 hours with up to twelve 200W panels.
 One caution for long series strings: a panel’s open-circuit voltage rises in cold weather. Keep a safety margin under the 280V limit of the high-voltage input, especially on a frosty morning. BLUETTI also notes that a rooftop array must stay within the input’s voltage, current and power limits, and may need extra equipment and professional installation.
 Runtime Estimates: What 2,560Wh Actually Powers 
 These are calculated estimates for one Apex 200 without expansion, with a 0.85 factor for conversion losses.
 Runtime (hours) ≈ 2,560Wh × 0.85 ÷ load (W) About 2,176Wh usable 
 🧊 Refrigerator

 ❄️ Chest freezer

 🔥 Space heater

about 1,400W while running
 That last line matters for RV owners. A rooftop air conditioner drains a single Apex 200 in about an hour and a half of compressor time. With one B500K, that stretches to about 4.7 hours. Appliances cycle on and off, so real runtimes are usually longer than these figures. To run your own list, use our power station runtime calculator .
 Expansion: B300K, B500K and Hub A1 
 BLUETTI gives the Apex 200 three ways to grow:
 B300K (2,764.8Wh): the smaller add-on battery. BLUETTI’s B300K tab on the Apex 200 page covers both the Apex 200 and the Apex 300, and the B300K for Apex lists at $1,099. Six of them take one Apex 200 to about 19.1kWh, by our math.
 B500K (5,120Wh): the larger one. One B500K brings the system to 7.68kWh , six bring it to 33.28kWh . Our BLUETTI B500K expansion battery review covers it in detail.
 Hub A1: links two or three Apex 200 units. Three units with eighteen B500K batteries reach 6,000W and 99.84kWh , according to BLUETTI.
 Adding a battery also lifts the output from 3,200W to 3,600W , and the maximum input from 3,200W to 4,600W. BLUETTI’s manual lists the B300 Pro, B300K, B500 Pro and B500K as compatible, and advises against mixing battery models. The B500K is easiest to buy in an Apex 200 bundle, which avoids any doubt about the version. The Hub A1, cables and batteries are otherwise sold separately.
 How It Compares to Other 2.5-3kWh Stations 
 Live prices for the Apex 200 and its closest alternatives:
 Model Capacity / output Price now Per kWh Lowest tracked Link

 3,072Wh · 3,600W $1,299 $1,599 -19% $423 $1,199 (Oct 8) Check deal Extra 5% off with code BPHUB5

 Prices come from each brand's US store and refresh automatically every few hours (oldest check on this table: Nov 4, 6:59 PM ET). Sale prices can change within the hour; the price in your cart is the one that counts. Prices, not coupon codes: some stores stack extra member or sign-up discounts at checkout.
 Apex 200 vs Anker SOLIX F2600
 The Anker SOLIX F2600 holds exactly the same 2,560Wh and also has a TT-30 outlet. On paper, the Apex 200 is ahead on output (3,200W against 2,400W), solar input (3,000W against 1,000W) and weight (59.3 lb against 69.7 lb). Both carry a 5-year warranty . The F2600 was listed as sold out on Anker’s store when we checked on November 4, 2026.
 Apex 200 vs EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra offers more capacity (3,072Wh) and more output (3,600W, with an X-Boost mode for loads up to 4,600W). EcoFlow publishes a 10ms auto-switch and up to 5 years of warranty with app registration, against 15ms and 5 years for the Apex 200. It sells for $1,299. The Apex 200’s edge is its solar input, its built-in RV ports and its expansion path to 33kWh.
 Who Should Buy the Apex 200 
 RV owners with a 30A hookup who also want home backup
 The TT-30R, the Anderson port and alternator charging make the Apex 200 one of the most RV-ready stations in its class. The same unit then comes inside when a storm takes the grid down.
 Solar-first users who need to move their station
 3,000W of solar input on a 59.3 lb unit is rare. If you camp off-grid or keep a station at a cabin, the Apex 200 refills fast from a modest array.
 Buyers who want to start small and grow
 Start with 2.56kWh, add a B500K when your needs grow, then a second unit if you want more power. Few 2.5kWh stations offer that much headroom.
 Who Should Skip It 
 Homes that need 240V
 For a well pump, central air or an electric dryer, look at the Apex 300, or at a 240V system from our best new BLUETTI power stations of 2026 .
 50A RV owners
 A 50A coach runs on two 120V legs. The Apex 200 feeds one, through a 30A plug. It will run the essentials through an adapter, but not the whole rig.
 Anyone who wants a station that rolls
 At 59.3 lb with no built-in wheels, the Apex 200 is not a grab-and-go unit. If you move your station often without a trolley, look at something smaller in our BLUETTI guides .
 Price, Bundles and Availability 
 The Apex 200 opened for orders on November 4, 2026 at 6 PM PST . It lists at $1,099. When sales opened, BLUETTI showed $1,099 against a $1,399 list price , which works out to about $429 per kWh. For reference, the Apex 300 sells for $1,499.
 BLUETTI also sells launch bundles. These were the prices shown on November 4, 2026:
 Bundle Price on November 4, 2026 
 Apex 200 + Charger 2 $1,598 
 Apex 200 + 500W panel $1,849 
 Apex 200 + B300K $2,199 
 Apex 200 + B500K + 30A TT-30 AC charging cable $2,799 
 Apex 200 + 2 × B300K $3,199 
 BLUETTI notes that the 500W panel and the 30A cable ship in late November, and that the 350W panel in other bundles ships on November 9.
 Check the Apex 200 price on BLUETTI 
 Compare it head to head: Anker F3000 vs BLUETTI Apex 200 · Apex 200 vs Apex 300 · Apex 200 vs Elite 300 · BLUETTI Apex 200 vs EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus · BLUETTI Apex 200 vs EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra · BLUETTI Apex 200 vs EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Classic · BLUETTI Apex 200 vs Jackery HomePower 3000 · All comparisons 
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Is the BLUETTI Apex 200 on sale now? Yes. The Apex 200 opened for orders on BLUETTI’s US store on November 4, 2026 at 6 PM PST.
 How much does the Apex 200 cost? When sales opened on November 4, 2026, BLUETTI listed the Apex 200 at $1,099 against a $1,399 list price. Bundles with batteries, panels or the Charger 2 cost more. Check BLUETTI’s store for the current price.
 Does the Apex 200 support 240V? No. The Apex 200 is 120V only, with three NEMA 5-20R outlets and one TT-30R. For 240V appliances, BLUETTI points buyers to the Apex 300, which has a NEMA 14-50R outlet.
 Can the Apex 200 power a 30A RV? Yes. Its TT-30R outlet takes a standard 30A RV plug. It delivers 3,200W on its own, or up to 3,600W with an expansion battery connected, so avoid running several large appliances at once.
 How far can the Apex 200 expand? One Apex 200 accepts up to six B300K or B500K batteries, for up to 33.28kWh with B500K units. Three Apex 200 units linked through the Hub A1 reach 6,000W and 99.84kWh, according to BLUETTI.
 What warranty does the Apex 200 have? BLUETTI lists a 5-year warranty for the Apex 200, the same as the Apex 300. The unit weighs 59.3 lb (26.9 kg) and measures 20.67 × 12.87 × 8.31 in.
 Final Verdict 
 The BLUETTI Apex 200 takes what works on the Apex 300, fast charging and serious expansion, and reshapes it for people who move their power around. It is 29% lighter , takes 25% more solar and has the RV ports built in . The trade-off is clear: no 240V and a little less output.
 The launch price makes the case stronger: on November 4, 2026, it cost $400 less than the Apex 300, with the same 5-year warranty. For RV owners who also want solid outage backup at home, it is one of the most interesting BLUETTI launches of 2026. Our rating: 8.5/10 , based on BLUETTI’s published specifications and launch price. We will revisit it when owner data are available.
